title: Rolle to Zurich: the Rhythm that Left Dalcroze for Laban
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Rolle, Lake Geneva, birth in the pharmacist's house
stops.campa: In the small vineyard town of Rolle on the north shore of Lake Geneva, Suzanne Perrottet is born to Émile Jules Perrottet, the town pharmacist, and Adèle Julie Amélie Simon, educated at the Königin-Katharina-Stift in Stuttgart. The household is musical before it is anything else: her sister Lili will become a violinist, and Suzanne herself is set before a small violin at four. Between the lake, the vines climbing behind the house, and her mother's German-trained ear, the girl who will unteach Europe how to dance to counted time is given, first, absolute pitch.
suggested_refs: The lakefront of Rolle, Vaud, where the Perrottet pharmacy stood

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatoire, Henri Marteau's violin class
stops.campa: By eight she is admitted to the class of Henri Marteau at the Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, the youngest bow among the older students. She practices solfège and violin with the ferocious discipline of a child who has been told she is gifted and believes it. The Conservatoire's stone rooms on the Place Neuve will shape the ear that later notates whole systems of rhythm by ear alone. Geneva, city of clocks, gives her the metronome; it will take Rudolf von Laban, on a mountain, to take it away again.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire de Musique de Genève, Place Neuve

stops.name: Geneva, Edvard Grieg at the Perrottet table
stops.campa: The Perrottet household keeps company with the touring musicians who pass through Geneva, and among the visitors the canon remembers is Edvard Grieg himself, received at the family table while Suzanne is still a girl at her scales. She grows up believing that composers are neighbors and concert halls are simply rooms one walks into. It is an inheritance of proximity to greatness that will recur all her life: Dalcroze, Laban, Schönberg by reputation, Jung and Bircher-Benner as her own later referring physicians, each in turn treating her as a colleague, not a pupil.
suggested_refs: Edvard Grieg, portrait photograph, c. 1900

stops.name: Geneva, Dalcroze's classes, the absolute ear
stops.campa: At the Conservatoire, Émile Jaques-Dalcroze is teaching solfège his own strange way: walking the beat, breathing the phrase, making the whole body count instead of the foot alone. Perrottet, equipped with absolute pitch, follows him into the new method and begins, on her own initiative, to write down its principles as he improvises them: the first notation she will ever keep. Dalcroze notices the ear that can transcribe him faster than he can speak. She becomes, informally, his private secretary of rhythm before she is twenty.
suggested_refs: Émile Jaques-Dalcroze at the Geneva Conservatoire, portrait c. 1905

stops.name: Solothurn, the first public demonstration
stops.campa: Dalcroze begins sending his best pupils out to demonstrate the method before the skeptical and the curious, and Perrottet, not yet seventeen, is among the first to walk a Swiss stage counting bars aloud with her whole spine. Solothurn's burghers watch young women march, skip and freeze on the beat of a piano they cannot see, and do not know they are watching the seed of an art that has no name yet. She is a demonstration piece herself: proof that a body can be taught to think in rhythm before it thinks in steps.
suggested_refs: Early Dalcroze eurhythmics demonstration photographs, Switzerland, c. 1906

stops.name: Paris, the demonstration before the Academy
stops.campa: The circuit widens to Paris, where the Dalcroze pupils perform before an academic audience more used to judging conservatoire recitals than watching young women translate Beethoven into gesture. Perrottet is praised for the exactness of her counting and the seriousness with which she treats what other cities still find a curiosity. The city that will one day watch the Ballets Russes reinvent the stage gets its first look, unregarded, at eurhythmics, a Swiss export that a handful of the avant-garde in the room quietly recognize as the coming thing.
suggested_refs: Jaques-Dalcroze eurhythmics demonstration programs, Paris, 1900s

stops.name: Basel, the disciple's circuit continues
stops.campa: In Basel the demonstrations draw teachers and physicians as much as artists: the method is already being read as therapy as well as pedagogy, a way of correcting stiff or anxious bodies through counted movement. Perrottet performs the improvisation exercises that will one day become her own vocabulary independent of Dalcroze: plastique animée, the body composing its own phrase against the music rather than merely walking it. The seed of her later break is already visible to anyone watching closely: she is improvising more than she is illustrating.
suggested_refs: Dalcroze eurhythmics 'plastique animée' demonstration photographs

stops.name: Amsterdam, the demonstration on the canal ring
stops.campa: By Amsterdam she is no longer a pupil among pupils but a name Dalcroze can send abroad on her own authority, teaching as much as demonstrating. She is twenty; her Conservatoire studies are finished; the rhythmic method has become her profession rather than an accomplishment. Within a year Dalcroze himself will summon his best teachers to a single garden city outside Dresden to build a permanent home for the work, and Perrottet, veteran of six cities' skepticism turned to applause, is among the first he calls.
suggested_refs: Jaques-Dalcroze eurhythmics demonstration photographs, Netherlands, 1909

stops.name: Dresden, the Ständehaus classes begin
stops.campa: Before Hellerau's own building exists, Dalcroze's Dresden courses meet in the Ständehaus on the Brühlsche Terrasse above the Elbe, and Perrottet teaches there through the winter of 1910, directing improvisation courses and playing violin in the school's own string quartet by night. She is now teacher and performer at once: the two halves of her life that Laban will later fuse into one act, dancing. For two more years she is Dalcroze's woman in Dresden, the most trusted hand in the whole German operation.
suggested_refs: The Ständehaus, Brühlsche Terrasse, Dresden

stops.name: Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt opens
stops.campa: The garden city north of Dresden opens its Bildungsanstalt für Musik und Rhythmus, reformed architecture built to house a reformed body, and Perrottet moves from the Ständehaus into its studios as one of the senior instructors, the same building where, within the year, a diligent and mutinous beginner named Mary Wigman will drill under her. She teaches improvisation and rhythm and keeps her violin under her chin between classes. Hellerau is Dalcroze's utopia made concrete: glass, light, undressed feet, and music made visible in a hundred moving bodies at once.
suggested_refs: The Festspielhaus Hellerau, temple of the rhythmic education
mary_wigman.journey.json, 'Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt of Jaques-Dalcroze' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Moscow, the Dalcroze demonstration tour
stops.campa: Dalcroze sends her east on a demonstration tour into Russia, into salons already restless with Ballets Russes talk and Scriabin's colored light. Perrottet teaches the counted body to audiences who will, within a decade, dissolve their own theatre into revolution. She returns from Moscow exhausted in a way the earlier circuit never left her: the method that made her has begun, quietly, to feel like a cage of correct beats. The overwork of the tour will send her, within months, to a sanatorium bed she does not yet know is the hinge of her whole life.
suggested_refs: Jaques-Dalcroze method demonstration tour, Russia, 1912
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Hellerau, the Festspielhaus, the great festival
stops.campa: In the new Festspielhaus, lit by Adolphe Appia's diffused and shadowless light, Hellerau stages the festival that will make its name across Europe: audiences from Diaghilev to Shaw to Kafka cross the continent to see rhythm made architecture. Perrottet performs among the massed pupils, one instrument in a machine built to prove that music can be seen. She is at the summit of the Dalcroze system's public triumph, and does not yet know that within six months a word spoken by a painter will begin to pull her out of it.
suggested_refs: The Festspielhaus Hellerau, 1912 festival photographs
mary_wigman.journey.json, 'Hellerau, the Festspielhaus, dance as the handmaid of music' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Weißer Hirsch, Dresden, the sanatorium bed beside Laban's
stops.campa: Run down by the tour, she takes a cure at the Lahmann-Sanatorium on the Weißer Hirsch above Dresden, and finds, convalescing in the same corridors, a Hungarian architect turned dance-visionary named Rudolf von Laban, himself collapsed from overwork building a rival system to Dalcroze's own. The canon remembers the meeting as a thunderclap disguised as bed rest: two exhausted reformers of the body, discovering between them that music and movement need not be married at all. She leaves the sanatorium cured of her fever and infected, permanently, with his heresy.
suggested_refs: The Lahmann-Sanatorium, Weißer Hirsch, Dresden, early 20th-century postcard
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Munich, the break from music
stops.campa: Star pupil of Jaques-Dalcroze at Hellerau, she comes to Laban's circle in Munich and defects from eurhythmics to his camp: from movement obeying music to movement sovereign. Around them gathers the first company, musicians, painters, seekers, and Laban formulates the heresy that founds the new German dance: rhythm lives in the body before it lives in sound. Perrottet, who has spent seven years teaching bodies to count, begins learning to let hers stop counting. The Dalcroze school takes note of the apostasy of its most trusted teacher.
suggested_refs: Suzanne Perrottet photographs, Munich period
laban.journey.json, 'Munich, Suzanne Perrottet and the break from music' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Hellerau, the declaration to Nolde and Wigman
stops.campa: She returns once more to the garden city to settle her affairs with Dalcroze and finds herself, in the studio, telling the painter Emil Nolde and the still-loyal pupil Mary Wigman exactly why she is leaving: for a man on a mountain above Ascona who lets his students dance with no music at all. The sentence passes into the annals of German dance as the annunciation that sends Wigman herself to Laban within the year. Perrottet does not know, saying it, that she is handing another woman the words that will end her own oldest friendship's rivalry.
stops.quote: Und die Perrottet sagte, sie verläßt Dalcroze und geht zu einem Mann, der tolle Sachen macht, der ganz ohne Musik, seine Schüler ganz ohne Musik tanzen läßt.
stops.quote_source: Mary Wigman, late recollection of 1913, cited at gusto-graeser.info, 'Mary Wigman', reporting Perrottet's own words
suggested_refs: Emil Nolde, Kerzentänzerinnen (Candle Dancers, 1912)
mary_wigman.journey.json, 'Hellerau, Emil Nolde speaks the word Laban' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin and quote)

stops.name: Vienna, the Dalcroze school she is given leave to found
stops.campa: In a last act of the old loyalty, Dalcroze grants his departing teacher his own blessing to open a school of his method in Vienna: proof that the break, however total it will become, begins as a parting in good faith rather than a scandal. She teaches the counted body one final season in the city of Freud and the Secession, drawing income and cover for what is already, privately, a different education: letters to and from Ascona, plans for a mountain she has not yet climbed.
suggested_refs: Dalcroze eurhythmics school, Vienna, 1913 announcement
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Monte Verità, Ascona, arrival on the sacred hill
stops.campa: She climbs the hill above Lake Maggiore where vegetarians, anarchists, sun-worshippers and theosophists have built a republic of the reformed body, and enters Laban's School for Art as his companion and first true collaborator, not his pupil. Bare feet, sun-cult robes, the prophet Gusto Gräser's grotto below the meadow: the whole colony seems built to receive exactly the apostasy she has just committed. She has spent seven years perfecting the counted step. On this hill she will spend the rest of her youth unlearning it.
suggested_refs: Monte Verità, Casa Anatta
laban.journey.json, 'Monte Verità, Ascona, arrival on the sacred hill' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Monte Verità, Wigman climbs the hill behind her
stops.campa: Three weeks after her own arrival, Perrottet watches the sentence she spoke at Hellerau bear its fruit: Mary Wigman climbs the same path to enroll in Laban's summer course, drawn by the very words Perrottet gave Nolde. The two former Dalcroze women meet again on the mountain, no longer teacher's colleagues but co-conspirators in an art with no name. Laban now has his two strongest instruments in one meadow: the collaborator who brought him the fire, and the disciple the fire was lit to attract.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Laban's dance farm on Monte Verità, 1913-14
mary_wigman.journey.json, 'Monte Verità, the climb to Laban' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Monte Verità, the daimon unbound, the encounter as liberating blow
stops.campa: Barefoot on the meadow, she dances for the first time to nothing but breath and gong and the swing of her own weight: the vocabulary of Ausdruckstanz smelted in real time between them. Later chroniclers of the school will call the whole encounter with Laban ein befreiender Schlag, a liberating blow, and this is its floor: tension and release, fall and recovery, music no longer required to authorize a single motion. The violinist who once notated Dalcroze's counted phrases faster than he could speak them now moves to no count at all.
suggested_refs: Johann Adam Meisenbach's photographs of Laban's Monte Verità circle, 1914
sources: Nimbus Verlag, 'Die Befreiung des Körpers: Suzanne Perrottet, Dada, Tanzen und der Monte Verità'

segments.name: The Dance Farm and the War

stops.name: Monte Verità, the dance farm, the little kingdom
stops.campa: The second summer on the mountain: Laban's little kingdom is a working dance farm where the company gardens, cooks, weaves its own costumes and dances, art and life composted together, and Perrottet, musician, teacher, now lover and collaborator, stands at the practical center of it, keeping the school running while Laban theorizes. She and Wigman deepen the movement experiments: swings, scales, the first sketches of a harmony of space modeled on crystals. It is the last summer of the old European peace, though no one on the mountain yet knows it.
suggested_refs: Laban's dancers photographed at harvest on the Monte Verità dance farm, summer 1914
laban.journey.json, 'Monte Verità, the dance farm, the little kingdom' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)
sources: Green, Mountain of Truth: The Counterculture Begins, Ascona 1900-1920

stops.name: Ascona, August 1914, the war breaks over the hill
stops.campa: The guns of Sarajevo's June echo down to the lake, and by August the frontiers close around the mountain: the international colony that made Monte Verità possible is suddenly a scatter of enemy nationals. Laban, a subject of Austria-Hungary, cannot simply cross into hostile France or Italy; the school must winter in neutral Switzerland. Perrottet, a Swiss citizen, becomes the practical passport of the whole operation: the one member of the household who can move freely across the borders now sealing around everyone she has just chosen to live with.
suggested_refs: laban.journey.json, 'Ascona, August 1914, the war breaks over the hill' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Zurich, the wartime school of dance, sound and word
stops.campa: Laban moves the work to Zurich, neutral hive of exiles, spies and prophets, and opens a school of dance, sound and word with Perrottet running its daily life while he sits over graph paper hunting the alphabet of movement. She teaches, keeps the books, plays violin for classes that Dalcroze himself would no longer recognize as his method's descendant. The city fills with every avant-garde that war has washed out of Europe, and the poor, cold, incandescent studio becomes the laboratory where Ausdruckstanz is refined from mountain rite into transferable discipline.
suggested_refs: Laban school Zurich photographs
laban.journey.json, 'Zurich, the wartime school' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)

stops.name: Hombrechtikon, the Labangarten, the triangular household
stops.campa: Beyond the city, in the orchards above the lake at Hombrechtikon, the household takes rural form: Laban, his wife Maja Lederer, their children, and Perrottet under one roof, an arrangement the canon records without scandal as a largely harmonious triangle. Here the school grows its own vegetables and its own theory at once: reform dress, handcraft, music theory, movement, taught to whoever will come. It is a commune before the word is fashionable, built on the working conviction that a dance reborn needs a life reborn to carry it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Laban household at Hombrechtikon, 1915-16
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Hombrechtikon: Allar is born
stops.campa: On the last day of January, Perrottet bears Laban a son, Allar, later known as André Perrottet von Laban, into the same orchard household where Laban's wife's own children are already growing up. The canon does not soften the arrangement into a lesser story: Allar will inherit both names and, in time, both arts, becoming himself a dancer, choreographer and sculptor before his death in 1956. For Perrottet the birth is the deepest root her defection from Dalcroze will ever put down: flesh where the others left only technique.
suggested_refs: André Perrottet von Laban, portrait photograph
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.
Archives Hub, 'Laban, Allar (b. 1916), Rudolf Laban's son by Suzanne Perrottet'

segments.name: Zurich: the Laban School and the Dada Door

stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1, the atonal mission
stops.campa: Five doors from Lenin's lodging, Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire draws Laban's dancers into its orbit: Sophie Taeuber, Käthe Wulff and Perrottet among the masks by Janco and the noise-poems read at the counter. Perrottet's own weapon is the piano: she gives the Dadaists the one thing none of them can supply for themselves, contemporary concert music, playing whole soirées of Schoenberg and Satie to ears that find it merely grotesque. The atlas's only Dada door opens here: abstract dance and atonal sound trading a single stage on the Spiegelgasse.
stops.quote: Das war meine Rolle bei den Dadaisten, die ganz moderne, neuzeitliche Musik dem Publikum vorführen. So spielte ich an etlichen Dada-Soiréen ausschliesslich Werke im atonalen Stil. Dem damaligen Publikum war diese Musik völlig unbekannt und kam ihnen für ihre Ohren grässlich vor.
stops.quote_source: Suzanne Perrottet, Ein bewegtes Leben, cited in 'Wie klang Dada?', Republik, 17 February 2022
suggested_refs: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1
Marcel Janco masks
laban.journey.json, 'Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1, the Dada adjacency' (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pin)

stops.name: Kaufleuten, Zurich, the soirées continue
stops.campa: As the war drags on and the Dada evenings outgrow the Spiegelgasse cellar, they move to larger halls like the Kaufleuten, and Perrottet's atonal programs move with them, still the resident modernist among the noise-poets and mask-dancers. She is, by now, the connective tissue between two entirely separate revolutions happening in the same small city: the abolition of music in dance on one side of town, the abolition of sense in poetry on the other, and her own two hands at the keyboard translating Schoenberg into the gap between them.
suggested_refs: Zurich Dada soirée programs, 1917-18, Kaufleuten and Zunfthaus venues

stops.name: Monte Verità, Sang an die Sonne, the sun sung down and up
stops.campa: At the close of the great wartime congress on the mountain, Laban stages Sang an die Sonne across a whole night: the sun's descent danced at evening over the lake, the demons of midnight before Gräser's grotto, at dawn a choir greeting the sun as promise that the war will end. Perrottet dances among the torches, no longer the arriving collaborator of 1913 but a co-founder of the whole language being performed, priestess of a religion of the body she helped compose, while the guns still hold Europe beyond the lake.
suggested_refs: Sang an die Sonne, Monte Verità, August 1917, photographs of the torch-lit hymn
mary_wigman.journey.json / laban.journey.json, same festival, shared pin (Colegio Invisible atlas)

stops.name: Zurich, Laban leaves, and the school becomes hers
stops.campa: At the end of the war Laban leaves Switzerland for Germany, where a shattered nation is hungry for exactly the choreographed mass-movement he can supply. He leaves behind the Zurich school, then housed in rooms borrowed from the Kunsthaus, and the woman who has kept its accounts, taught its classes and borne its founder's son. Perrottet takes over outright. What began as Dalcroze's Bildungsanstalt and became Laban's laboratory now becomes, without ceremony, simply hers: six decades of teaching about to begin under a single continuous roof.
suggested_refs: Kunsthaus Zürich, early premises of the Laban/Perrottet school
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the Schule für Eurythmie, renamed against confusion
stops.campa: She continues the school first jointly with Käthe Wulff under the name Schule für Eurythmie, and is soon forced to rename it again, since the word eurythmy has by now been claimed by Rudolf Steiner's anthroposophical movement for an entirely different discipline. The confusion of names tells its own story: an idea born of Dalcroze, refined by Laban, and now sovereign under Perrottet, must keep re-declaring what it is not in order to be recognized for what it is. It will eventually settle as simply the Bewegungsschule Suzanne Perrottet.
suggested_refs: Bewegungsschule Suzanne Perrottet, early letterhead and programs
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the lecture on the neglected body
stops.campa: She lectures publicly under the title Der vernachlässigte Körper und seine Forderungen, the neglected body and its demands, carrying the mountain's doctrine down into the language of civic reform: posture, breath and unhurried movement as public health, not merely artistic mysticism. Physicians in the audience take note; within a decade doctors like Max Bircher-Benner and even Carl Gustav Jung will be referring patients directly to her studio. Perrottet has found the form her whole career will take: dance as medicine for a century that broke its own body in the trenches.
suggested_refs: 'Der vernachlässigte Körper und seine Forderungen', lecture text, 1921
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, Gluck's Iphigénie en Aulide, danced whole
stops.campa: She choreographs Christoph Willibald Gluck's Iphigénie en Aulide for the Zurich stage, turning her mountain vocabulary, tension, release, weight given and taken back, toward the eighteenth-century opera repertoire that Dalcroze himself once used to teach counted phrasing. The commission is a quiet act of reconciliation and conquest at once: the master she left is honored in the very medium she abandoned him for, danced now to music instead of against its absence, since even the sovereign body, she has learned, need not always dance in silence.
suggested_refs: Zurich Stadttheater, Iphigénie en Aulide production records, 1923
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the Perrottet-Schoop years
stops.campa: For two years the school runs jointly with the young dancer Trudi Schoop, briefly renamed Bewegungsschule Perrottet-Schoop, a partnership between the mountain's first generation and its next. Schoop will go on to a career in grotesque and comic dance far from Laban's high seriousness, but she takes from Perrottet's studio the same root discipline every pupil here receives: the body trusted to invent its own necessity. Among the other names Perrottet trains in these years are Max Terpis and Vera Skoronel, both bound for their own places in the same expanding atlas of German dance.
suggested_refs: Bewegungsschule Perrottet-Schoop, program, 1927-29
vera_skoronel.journey.json (Colegio Invisible atlas, shared pupil)
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the Zett-Haus, the school's futurist home
stops.campa: The school moves into the newly built Zett-Haus at Badenerstrasse 18, a startling glass-and-steel modernist block by the architects Flora Steiger-Crawford and Rudolf Steiger, a building as programmatically new as the movement taught inside it. Perrottet's studio takes its place among the building's other progressive tenants, the reformed body now housed in reformed architecture just as it was at Hellerau twenty years before, only this time the architecture and the choreography answer to no master but her.
suggested_refs: Zett-Haus, Badenerstrasse 18, Zurich, built 1930-32

stops.name: Lausanne, teaching the engineers to move
stops.campa: She is engaged to teach rhythmic gymnastics, body language and musical accompaniment at the École Polytechnique in Lausanne: precision-trained engineers sent to a dance pedagogue descended from Dalcroze and Laban both, to learn what their slide rules cannot give them. It is a strange late loop of her own itinerary: the canton where she was born, teaching the same discipline of counted and then uncounted movement to a generation that will build Switzerland's postwar infrastructure with hands she has, in some measure, first taught to be present in space.
suggested_refs: École Polytechnique de l'Université de Lausanne, 1930s campus

stops.name: Zurich, the Landesausstellung of 1939
stops.campa: At the legendary Swiss National Exhibition on the Zürichhorn, the Landi, the great patriotic pageant mounted as Europe rearms around a determinedly neutral Switzerland, Perrottet's pupils perform, her movement pedagogy folded for one bright summer into the nation's own self-portrait. Forty years after the folk fair scenes of her own childhood on Lake Geneva, she stands inside a much larger and more anxious festival, teaching bodies to move well in a country trying to convince itself, and everyone else, that it will not be swallowed by the war massing at its borders.
suggested_refs: Schweizerische Landesausstellung 1939, Zürichhorn, photographs
sources: Nimbus Verlag, 'Die Befreiung des Körpers: Suzanne Perrottet, Dada, Tanzen und der Monte Verità'

stops.name: Zurich, the Swiss Professional Association founded
stops.campa: The same year, she co-founds the Schweizerischer Berufsverband für Tanz und Gymnastik, the Swiss professional association for dance and gymnastics, and sits on its committee for the next sixteen years. The itinerant art she once demonstrated on borrowed stages from Solothurn to Moscow now has a licensing body, a professional standard, a seat at the table of Swiss cultural bureaucracy. The revolutionary of Monte Verità has become, without renouncing anything, an institution: the surest sign a heresy has actually won.
suggested_refs: Schweizerischer Berufsverband für Tanz und Gymnastik, founding documents, 1939
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the Mühlebachstrasse studio, the long afternoon
stops.campa: In the postwar decades her practice settles into a studio on the Mühlebachstrasse in Riesbach, where she teaches dancers, actors, children and adults, including pupils with physical and mental disabilities, alongside her ongoing private research into notation and the archive of photographs she has kept since Hellerau. Doctors still send her patients; theatres still send her actors; the mountain's old promise that movement could be sovereign has become, in this quiet Zurich street, simply a decades-long clinical and pedagogical practice, unglamorous and exact.
suggested_refs: Suzanne Perrottet teaching in her Zurich studio, photographs, 1950s-60s
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, the school closes, sixty years ended
stops.campa: At ninety, Perrottet closes the school she has run continuously, first jointly, then alone, under three successive names, since taking it from Laban's hands in the winter of 1918. Sixty-one years of pupils have passed through it: Wigman's fellow travelers, Schoop, Terpis, Skoronel, and generations of ordinary Zurich children and convalescents besides. No single institution in the atlas of German-speaking modern dance runs so long under one continuous teacher. She has outlived Dalcroze, outlived Laban, and outlived, by decades, almost everyone else who stood with her on the mountain in 1913.
suggested_refs: Bewegungsschule Suzanne Perrottet, closing notice, 1979
sources: Biografie von Suzanne Perrottet, Sächsische Biografie, ISGV e.V.

stops.name: Zurich, telling the moving life to Giorgio Wolfensberger
stops.campa: In her nineties, Perrottet sits for the photographer and filmmaker Giorgio J. Wolfensberger across two years of recorded conversation, entrusting him with her memories and her entire photographic archive: Hellerau, Monte Verità, Cabaret Voltaire, sixty years of Zurich pupils, all of it dictated onto tape before it can be lost. The recordings will become Ein bewegtes Leben and, later, the illustrated Die Befreiung des Körpers: a woman who spent her working life teaching bodies to remember movement without notation, at the end entrusting her own life's movement to someone else's pen.
stops.quote: Das war meine Rolle bei den Dadaisten, die ganz moderne, neuzeitliche Musik dem Publikum vorführen.
stops.quote_source: Suzanne Perrottet, Ein bewegtes Leben (recorded interviews with Giorgio J. Wolfensberger, 1981-83)

stops.name: Zurich, death at ninety-three
stops.campa: Suzanne Perrottet dies in Zurich on the tenth of August, ninety-three years old, the last of the trio: Dalcroze's discipline, Laban's mountain, Wigman's fire, still standing when the others had long since passed into history's keeping. Her estate, photographs and letters go seven years later to the Kunsthaus Zürich library, the same institution whose borrowed rooms once housed the school she inherited from Laban in 1918. The rhythm she once notated by ear as a girl in Geneva has, by the time she lets it go, become an entire national dance tradition's grandmother.
